title: Maximilian Kolbe (1894–1941)
hookLine: in Auschwitz a Franciscan priest offers to die in place of a father of a family

cards: Before the war, he was a busy man: a Polish Franciscan friar with round glasses and a head full of plans.

He founded a friary near Warsaw that kept growing, ran printing presses, put out magazines, even started a radio station. He traveled to Japan and set up a friary there too. Then, in 1939, Germany invaded Poland.
The friary sheltered refugees, Jews among them. In 1941 he was arrested, and that May he was sent to Auschwitz, where he became a number, 16670.

teach.b: First, where we are. Auschwitz was the largest of the Nazi death camps. More than a million people were murdered there, and the great majority were Jews, killed because they were Jews.
Poles, Roma, Soviet prisoners and others died there too.
Kolbe was one prisoner among very many, and his story sits inside that much larger grief. In the summer of 1941, a man escaped from Kolbe's block.
As punishment, the camp's deputy commander lined the prisoners up and picked ten men to die by starvation in an underground cell.
One of them, a Polish sergeant named Franciszek Gajowniczek, cried out for his wife and his children.

teach.h: A PRIEST STEPS OUT OF LINE.
teach.b: Then Kolbe stepped out of the line. He said he was a Catholic priest, and asked to take that man's place. Nobody knows exactly why the officer agreed, but he did.
In the starvation cell, survivors said later, Kolbe led the men in prayers and hymns, and the cell was strangely calm. After two weeks, four were still alive, Kolbe among them.
On the fourteenth of August, 1941, they were killed with an injection. Gajowniczek survived the war.
He lived into his nineties, and he was in Saint Peter's Square in 1982 when Pope John Paul the Second declared Kolbe a saint and a martyr of charity.

teach.h: GREATER LOVE THAN THIS NO MAN HATH.
teach.b: Catholics hear in this the words of Jesus in the Douay-Rheims: "Greater love than this no man hath, that a man lay down his life for his friends." Kolbe hadn't known the man.

how: Catholics keep St. Maximilian Kolbe's feast on August 14, the day he died; he is honored as a patron of prisoners and families, and pilgrims pray at the cell in Auschwitz's Block 11 where he died.

practice: This isn't for feeling anything in particular; it's for remembering the millions murdered in the Holocaust, most of them Jews, whole families, whole towns.
Then think of one, a child, a grandmother, a name you may have read, and hold that one person for a while. If you pray, you can pray for the dead; if you don't, keep a silence for them.

wordCard.voice: Maximilian Kolbe. A Franciscan priest who, in Auschwitz, gave his life in place of a stranger with a family.

carryVoice: Your line: he stepped forward. One step out of a line, for a stranger. Go gently, and see you tomorrow.
